Notes

Adverse Events & Patient-Safety Incidents

KEY DEFINITIONS
Adverse event: a healthcare-related incident resulting in patient harm or worsening of condition, including postoperative complications.
Near miss: an incident with potential for unacceptable consequences that does not cause harm, only because of chance or timely prevention.

Patient-safety complications may arise from human, communication, system, environmental, medication, or procedural factors.

HIGH-YIELD
Inadequate communication between healthcare staff is one of the most common causes of adverse events / complications.
  • Near miss = an incident that could have caused unacceptable consequences but did not occur. 439
Inadequate communication between healthcare staff is one of the most common causes of adverse events / complications.
Notes

Causes of Adverse Events

Communication & Handover

Inadequate communication between junior/senior staff, multidisciplinary teams, patients, and families is a major source of error.
Proper endorsement/handover is essential: communicate the patient's condition, ongoing problems, management, and required follow-up.
Poor coordination during handovers can cause loss of continuity and serious complications.
Ensure a patient is never left without clear clinical responsibility/coverage.
Communicate openly with the patient and ensure they understand their condition.
Seek colleagues' opinions when uncertain; intraoperative assistants may spot findings the primary surgeon misses.
RULE OF THUMB
Early communication + early escalation/change of plan can prevent deterioration.
Notes

Human & Staffing Factors

Psychological/cognitive overload increases error risk.
Inadequate staffing or insufficient knowledge, clinical skills, operative skills, or experience compromises safety.
Clinicians performing unfamiliar procedures/technology require appropriate training and supervision (e.g. an inexperienced operator using advanced laparoscopic techniques).
Healthcare workers must understand the hospital's systems, resources, and procedures.
  • Example of a human factor: error in the use of investigations (staffing levels, similar drugs and new technology are counted under other factor groups in this question). 437
  • Same question in the final: human factor → error in doing an investigation. 437 Final
  • Laparoscopy with no CO₂ left — never insufflate oxygen (it supports combustion) or other gases: "Sorry, it is not safe." 435
Notes

System / Organizational Factors

Lack of clear procedures/protocols.
Inadequate staff coordination, supervision, or training.
Cost/resource policies may influence patient care.
Hospitals require an appropriate incident-reporting system; patient-safety incidents should be reported.
WARNING
If the institution lacks the necessary capacity, expertise, facilities, or equipment → escalate to administration and arrange appropriate referral/transfer.
Notes

Environment & Resources

Patient safety is affected by environment, infrastructure, and facility design. Risks include lack of:

Appropriate facilities
Equipment/instruments
Basic supplies (e.g. gloves)
Skilled expertise

ER and operating room are complex, high-risk environments where errors can have serious consequences.

Notes

Medical & Technological Complexity

Increasing medical complexity and use of new/advanced technology increase risk when personnel lack sufficient experience. Medication interactions/adverse effects may also contribute to complications.

  • Patient died from a medication interaction → first action as a provider: root cause analysis (find the system cause, don't punish individuals). 429 Final ×2
Notes

Medication Safety

Medication-related communication should clearly specify:

ElementWhy it matters
DrugExact agent being ordered/administered
DosePrevents under/overdosing
IndicationConfirms clinical rationale
DurationPrevents unnecessarily prolonged/short therapy
Route/administrationCorrect method of delivery
DANGER
Similar or related drugs may create prescribing/allergy risks. Penicillin/cephalosporin cross-allergy was highlighted at approximately 15%.
WARNING
Parenteral medication/infusion errors can be dangerous — always verify the correct drug, dose, route, concentration, and administration method (example discussed: an adrenaline infusion error).
Notes

Blood Transfusion Safety

HIGH-YIELD — HIGH RISK
Blood transfusion is a particularly high-risk process. Transfusion errors can cause severe complications and may be fatal.
Before transfusion, strictly confirm patient identity, including patient ID/name and blood-related identification details.
Monitor the patient clinically during transfusion, including pulse/vital signs.
Blood transfusion is a particularly high-risk process. Transfusion errors can cause severe complications and may be fatal.
Notes

Informed Consent & Patient Communication

CORE PRINCIPLE
Consent is a communication process, not merely signing a form. Documentation/coding or a signed form is never a substitute for adequate discussion.
  • Life-threatening emergency, nobody available → no consent needed (implied consent). 442 441 438 ×2
  • Universal precautions: never re-sheath needles — discard sharps directly in a sharps container. 438
Notes

What the Patient Must Understand

DomainDetail
DiagnosisDiagnosis or possible diagnosis, and current condition
PurposePurpose/goals of treatment or surgery
ProcedureDetails/nature of the planned procedure
RisksMaterial risks/possible complications
BenefitsExpected benefits
AlternativesAlternative treatment options, with advantages/disadvantages of each
OperatorWho is responsible for performing the operation
falsely presented as confirmed/cured). ablation.• The responsible surgeon/operator should obtain consent for the procedure they are expected to perform.
• Communicate risks in an understandable, balanced manner rather than unnecessarily frightening the patient.
• Do not present uncertain diagnoses or outcomes as definite (e.g. a suspected malignancy should be explained as a possibility, not
• Discuss reasonable alternatives even when less effective — e.g. for liver lesions/tumors: radiofrequency ablation and microwave
KEY RULE
The patient may change their mind/withdraw consent at any time before the procedure. Good communication matters — patients remember how complications and treatment discussions were handled.

| Purpose | Goals of treatment or surgery |

| Procedure | Details/nature of the planned procedure |

| Risks | Material risks/possible complications |

| Benefits | Expected benefits |

Notes

Professionalism & Surgical Competence

Core Competencies for Safe Practice

Knowledge
Clinical skills
Operative/technical skills
Clinical experience
Decision-making
Communication
Medical ethics & professionalism

Professionalism is essential throughout patient assessment and treatment.

  • A competent adult signs his own consent — his son cannot sign for him. 437 ×2
Notes

Decision-Making

Decision-making is a core surgical skill — technical ability alone is insufficient.

PhaseFocus
PreoperativePlanning, work-up, and consent decisions
IntraoperativeReal-time judgment as findings evolve
PostoperativeMonitoring, escalation, and follow-up decisions
When circumstances change: recognize the problem, communicate it, seek appropriate opinions, and modify management early.
Notes

Teamwork in the Operating Room

Encourage communication rather than silencing junior staff/assistants.
Other team members may recognize anatomy, complications, or technical problems from a different viewpoint.
Appropriate teamwork and speaking up can prevent operative errors.
Notes

Patient Assessment & Professional Conduct

Establish professional rapport: sit with the patient, obtain a proper history, examine them, and demonstrate appropriate attention to their concerns.
Perform a structured history + physical examination + relevant laboratory/investigative assessment before management.
Do not rely on tests while neglecting clinical examination (e.g. abdominal pathology requires proper inspection/examination for abnormalities such as abdominal distension and hernia).
Examination of female patients should follow appropriate professional practice with a nurse/chaperone present when required.
Patient dignity, consent, and professionalism remain important during examination.
  • The hazard class that deals with radiation, laser, furniture, floors, buildings and storage → keyed physical (physiological in one version) hazard. 429 Final 429 Final
Notes

Operative/Procedural Safety

Safe Technique

Follow the correct steps of the procedure/operation rather than proceeding without a structured technique.
Avoid aggressive tissue handling — excessive force/trauma causes tissue injury, bleeding, and excessive postoperative adhesions.
Surgical technique requires controlled, patient, gentle tissue handling.
Appropriate preparation before operating is essential.
SOURCES OF PROCEDURAL ERROR
Poor/inadequate preparation
Misinterpretation of findings
Incorrect technique
Misuse of surgical instruments
  • Wrong knee listed, site not yet marked → time-out/verification with the team and the patient, then mark the correct site. 442
Notes

Overall Patient-Safety Principle

BIG PICTURE
Preventing complications requires integration of communication, appropriate staffing/training, supervision, resources, accurate medication/transfusion practices, informed consent, sound clinical judgment, professionalism, teamwork, and careful operative technique.
Preventing complications = communication + staffing/training + supervision + resources + accurate medication/transfusion practice + informed consent + sound judgement + professionalism + teamwork + careful technique.
